title: Are mutants a valid substitute for real faults in software testing?
authors: Just, R.; Jalali, D.; Inozemtseva, L.; Ernst, M. D.; Holmes, R.; Fraser, G.
supporting_sentence: The results show a statistically significant correlation between mutant detection and real fault detection, independently of code coverage.
relevance: Foundational validity evidence that mutation score proxies real-fault detection; justifies treating mutation score as oracle strength.

title: Is mutation an appropriate tool for testing experiments?
authors: Andrews, J. H.; Briand, L. C.; Labiche, Y.
supporting_sentence: It is concluded that, based on the data available thus far, the use of mutation operators is yielding trustworthy results (generated mutants are similar to real faults).
relevance: Earliest controlled comparison of mutants vs real vs hand-seeded faults; grounds mutant representativeness claims.

title: Mutation Testing Advances: An Analysis and Survey
authors: Papadakis, M.; Kintis, M.; Zhang, J.; Jia, Y.; Le Traon, Y.; Harman, M.
supporting_sentence: The choice of mutation testing tool needs to be made carefully as at the current state, mutation testing tools differ significantly
relevance: Supplies the seven-point best-practice checklist our mutation protocol must satisfy (operators, tool, redundancy, suites, CPA, repetitions, granularity).

title: Mind the Gap: The Difference Between Coverage and Mutation Score Can Guide Testing Efforts
authors: Jain, K.; Kalburgi, G. T.; Le Goues, C.; Groce, A.
supporting_sentence: We performed no analysis to remove equivalent mutants, as our use of mutation scores is focused only on comparing differences across projects
relevance: Defines the oracle gap (coverage minus mutation score), the direct intellectual ancestor of our coverage-conditioning requirement.

title: Does mutation testing improve testing practices?
authors: Petrovic, G.; Ivankovic, M.; Fraser, G.; Just, R.
supporting_sentence: We found that for 1043 (70%) of the bugs, mutation testing would have reported a fault-coupled mutant in the bug-introducing change.
relevance: Industrial fault-coupling evidence at scale (1502 bugs); supports mutant representativeness in real repositories rather than toy programs.

title: Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: A view from Google
authors: Petrovic, G.; Ivankovic, M.; Fraser, G.; Just, R.
supporting_sentence: even when applying sampling techniques to substantially reduce the number of mutants, developers at Google initially classified 85% of reported mutants as unproductive
relevance: Evidence that raw mutation scores are dominated by unproductive mutants and are not actionable; motivates filtering and operator justification.

title: Threats to the validity of mutation-based test assessment
authors: Papadakis, M.; Henard, C.; Harman, M.; Jia, Y.; Le Traon, Y.
supporting_sentence: Our findings indicate that Type I errors occur, for arbitrary experiments that fail to take countermeasures, approximately 62% of the time.
relevance: Shows mutation-based comparisons are invalid unless redundant/subsumed mutants are controlled; a threat to validity we must explicitly address.

title: A study of equivalent and stubborn mutation operators using human analysis of equivalence
authors: Yao, X.; Harman, M.; Jia, Y.
supporting_sentence: PARAPHRASE: Of 4,181 generated mutants, 1,230 unkilled mutants were manually checked; 946 (approx. 23%) were found equivalent and 284 (approx. 7%) stubborn.
relevance: Human ground-truth equivalent-mutant prevalence by operator; tells us which operators to avoid and what equivalence rate to expect.

title: An Empirical Study on Mutation, Statement and Branch Coverage Fault Revelation that Avoids the Unreliable Clean Program Assumption
authors: Titcheu Chekam, T.; Papadakis, M.; Le Traon, Y.; Harman, M.
supporting_sentence: from which our primary finding is that strong mutation testing has the highest fault revelation of four widely-used criteria
relevance: Direct evidence that mutation score finds faults coverage misses; the empirical basis for a coverage-conditioned design.

title: Detecting Trivial Mutant Equivalences via Compiler Optimisations
authors: Kintis, M.; Papadakis, M.; Jia, Y.; Malevris, N.; Le Traon, Y.; Harman, M.
supporting_sentence: TCE equivalent mutants account for 7.4 and 5.7 percent of all C and Java mutants
relevance: Cheap automated equivalent/duplicate suppression (TCE) we can run before scoring; quantifies the residue that cannot be suppressed automatically.

title: Equivalent Mutants in the Wild: Identifying and Efficiently Suppressing Equivalent Mutants for Java Programs
authors: Kushigian, B.; Kaufman, S.; Featherman, R.; Potter, H.; Madadi, A.; Just, R.
supporting_sentence: the median equivalent mutant rate across the 7 projects is 2.97%
relevance: Most recent ground truth on equivalent-mutant prevalence in real Java projects; the number we cite for expected equivalence rate.

title: Mutation testing in the wild: findings from GitHub
authors: Sanchez, A. B.; Delgado-Perez, P.; Medina-Bulo, I.; Segura, S.
supporting_sentence: we first performed a search for mutation testing tools, 127 in total
relevance: Documents which mutation tools practitioners actually use (PIT, Infection, Humbug), grounding our tool choice in observed practice.

title: Mutta: a novel tool for E2E web mutation testing
authors: Leotta, M.; Paparella, D.; Ricca, F.
supporting_sentence: took into account the coverage information to consider only the mutants actually executed
relevance: Closest prior work measuring mutation score of end-to-end (system-level) suites, and it also conditions on coverage; bounds our novelty.

title: Static and Dynamic Comparison of Mutation Testing Tools for Python
authors: Guerino, L. R.; Kuroishi, P. H.; Paiva, A. C. R.; Vincenzi, A. M. R.
supporting_sentence: In this work, we evaluate (statically and dynamically) four Python mutation testing tools, namely CosmicRay, MutPy, MutMut, and Mutatest.
relevance: Shows Python mutation tools (incl. mutmut) are not interchangeable; supports a tool-comparability caveat for our Python stack.

title: How effective are mutation testing tools? An empirical analysis of Java mutation testing tools with manual analysis and real faults
authors: Kintis, M.; Papadakis, M.; Papadopoulos, A.; Valvis, E.; Malevris, N.; Le Traon, Y.
supporting_sentence: no tool is able to subsume the others
relevance: Direct cross-tool comparison (PIT, PIT-RV, MuJava, Major); the strongest published evidence that mutation scores are tool-dependent.

title: Do Redundant Mutants Affect the Effectiveness and Efficiency of Mutation Analysis?
authors: Just, R.; Kapfhammer, G. M.; Schweiggert, F.
supporting_sentence: redundant mutants can lead to a mutation score that is misleadingly overestimated by as much as 10%
relevance: Quantifies how redundancy inflates mutation score; grounds the requirement to report non-redundant operator sets.

title: Mutation Testing in Evolving Systems: Studying the Relevance of Mutants to Code Evolution
authors: Ojdanic, M.; Soremekun, E.; Degiovanni, R.; Papadakis, M.; Le Traon, Y.
supporting_sentence: Our analysis shows that commit-relevant mutants are located mainly outside of program commit change (81%)
relevance: Evidence on mutation over software evolution; warns that mutating only changed code misses most commit-relevant mutants, shaping our longitudinal design.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Manually Created Equivalent Mutants
authors: Straubinger, P.; Degenhart, A.; Fraser, G.
supporting_sentence: less than 10% of manually created mutants are equivalent
relevance: Human-produced mutants show a much lower equivalence rate than tool-produced ones; reinforces that equivalence prevalence is operator/tool dependent.
